opener.heading: Week 52: Reflection & Winter Holidays 🎄
about: The last full week of the year runs on what gets left behind. She presses a shoe sole into clay and keeps the shape it leaves. She stands photographs of everybody up on a covered table with greenery round the base. She wraps coins in foil, hides them, and draws a map so somebody else can find them. Each of those outlasts the hour that made it, and that is as close to looking back as four gets.

Three occasions land inside seven days. Hanukkah starts at sundown on Friday, so the menorah she builds that morning goes on the windowsill and gets lit before dinner. Christmas is Saturday, opened one parcel at a time with the rule holding for the adults too. Wednesday is your birthday, and Azlyn runs it: the frosting, the sprinkles, the card, the seating plan. Monday sits in the middle with three candle rules and a pan of cocoa, because this week has more open flame in it than any other week of the year.
azlyn: Three fire rules she can say back. Candles stay on the tray, only a grown-up strikes a match, tell a grown-up the moment something goes wrong.
Hiding something where somebody else will look. She sets Kreston's round at his height and finds out his view of the room is two feet lower than hers.
One object at two sizes. A Christmas toy built as tall as the door, then again small enough to shut in a matchbox, with the same parts list holding for both.
How a print gets left behind. Something soft takes the shape, the object goes away, the shape stays. She owns the sequence because her hands did every step of it.
Sorting, counting and naming her own groups. Candy into a muffin tin by categories she invents, counted out loud, labeled in her words.
you: Hiding something well means imagining another creature's point of view
Sorting living things is harder than sorting objects, because they move
Making it enormous is how she checks she knows the parts
Fire and flame need rules, not avoidance
A copy of a thing teaches her what a fossil is
Sorting the candy is more interesting to her than eating it
A photo on a table gives a dead person a place, and that helps her more than an explanation

days.title: Eight Nights Start Tonight
days.prepTonight: Mix the salt dough (1 cup flour, 1/2 cup salt, water a spoonful at a time) and leave it in the fridge, with the candles, foil and a jar lid on the table.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: Nine the Same and One Taller

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Hiding Place He Can Find

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Map of the Hiding Places

opening.title: Nine the Same and One Taller
opening.need: the salt dough or a tub of playdough · 1 metal baking tray · 1 ruler or a strip of card.
steps: Hand her the whole lump and let her pull it into nine pieces. The first pass comes out wild, so leave it.
Eight have to match. She rolls, compares two at a time in her palms, and moves dough between them until they agree.
The ninth takes everything left over and stands taller. Line all nine along the tray with the ruler and leave them until 9:15.

main.title: The Menorah on the Windowsill
materials: Salt dough (1 cup flour, 1/2 cup salt, water) or a tub of store playdough
9 candles (Hanukkah candles, or birthday candles as the substitute)
1 clean jar lid, to raise the shamash
1 ruler or a strip of card for spacing
steps: Cover the tray with foil and fold the edges under the rim to catch the wax.
Jar lid upside down near the middle, the tall lump pressed onto it. That is the shamash, the candle that lights the other eight.
Space the other eight with the ruler, four each side, pressing every lump flat-bottomed so it grips the foil.
She pushes one candle into each holder. Sight down the row and let her straighten the crooked ones.
Marker on the foil: number the holders right to left, the way the candles go in. Tonight one gets lit.
Carry it to the windowsill together, high and back from the curtain, ready for sundown.
main.tip: The shamash is the one with a job. She lifts it out unlit at sundown and hands it to you, you light it and stand it back on the lid, and she puts it away once the wax is cold.

outside.title: What's in Everybody's Window
paras: Walk the block looking up instead of down. Late December puts something behind most of the glass: a menorah on a sill, a tree lit at eleven in the morning, paper snowflakes taped up by somebody her size, a window with only a cat. Come home past the one with the most going on.

days.infant: Kreston is 18 months and pretend play has started, so he purses his lips and blows at the cold candles, copying Azlyn at every birthday this year. Give him a torn square of foil at the far end of the table to crush and flatten. He has 20-some words, and light is a good one to hand him while nothing is lit.

second.title: The Hiding Place He Can Find
second.intro: Hiding is her favorite game and she is bad at it, because she hides where she would look.
materials: 6 foil-wrapped chocolate coins, or ordinary coins wrapped in foil
3 soft items to hide for Kreston: a board book, a sock ball, a wooden spoon
Paper and a crayon for her map
steps: Three paper bags, a sticky note on each: Kreston, you, her.
Kreston's round first. She hides the board book, the sock ball and the wooden spoon at his height, in the open and half showing.
A sticky note on the wall above each one, so you can find them again when he cannot.
Let him loose with his bag. She watches him walk past two of the three.
Now the high round. Six foil coins for a grown-up: on top of the door frame, behind a book, under an upturned mug. She marks each on her paper with the crayon.
Hunt with your bag, saying every thought out loud. She gives three away and that is allowed.

Everything into the basket, counted against her map. Two coins go back out for a turn of her own while Kreston is in the high chair, and both come back into the basket before he is loose in the room again.
second.tip: The map is worth more than the coins. Date it and put it on the fridge.

alternatives: Hide one thing over and over in the same three places.
Wrap five objects in foil and guess each by shape.
Upturned cups on a tray, one coin under one.
Let Kreston hide something and time the hunt.
outAgain: A café with cake, and a window seat, because half the street is out and nobody is hurrying
The store for the one forgotten thing, before everything shuts at four
A slow drive round the neighborhood in the dark, lights only
Nowhere at all, if the day has enough in it

aroundWorld.title: The Last Days of the Year 🍇
paras: Plenty of the world eats its way out of the old year. Spanish families swallow twelve grapes on the twelve strokes of midnight, one wish per grape. Japanese households eat long buckwheat noodles on December 31 for a long life, and across the American South, black-eyed peas and greens go on the table on January 1, peas for coins and greens for folding money.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Count twelve grapes onto her plate tonight, quartered lengthwise, and eat them one at a time, one good thing from this year for each. Kreston's are cut the same way onto his own tray, a few at a time.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: Danish families save chipped plates all year and throw them at their friends' front doors on New Year's Eve. The biggest heap means the most friends.

days.krestonPM: At 18 months he finds things by walking into a room and looking, then carries them to whoever is nearest. Hide the board book in a new spot and he hunts it. The foil coins are not for him, so run his round first and sweep before he is down.

insight.headline: Hiding something well means imagining another creature's point of view.
paras: Azlyn has spent a year hiding a coin behind her back and telling you she cannot see it. Hiding for somebody else asks her to hold two pictures at once: the room as she sees it, and the room as Kreston sees it from two feet lower. Researchers call that theory of mind, and it builds in pieces between three and five. You have fed it all year without naming it, every time you said he is crying because he wanted the cup. A hunt she designs for one finder puts the same work in front of her with a prize on the end.

days.safety: Real candles burn on that windowsill tonight. Set the tray back from the curtain, behind something Kreston cannot climb, and stay in the room while they are lit. Never leave him alone with them. The foil-wrapped coins are a choking hazard at 18 months, so count them out and count them back into the basket.

days.title: The Rule That Holds for the Adults Too
days.prepTonight: Put a trash bag, a shallow box and a notebook by the tree tonight, and check every parcel has a name on it.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Who Else Is Out on Christmas Morning

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: One New Thing, on Her Own

opening.title: Whose Name Is On It
steps: She goes round the tree reading names she cannot read, matching first letters against the names you say out loud.
One pile per person. Hers gets counted four times and the count changes twice.
Write each name big on a sticky note, let her stick it on the right pile, and nothing gets opened until 9:15.

main.title: One Parcel at a Time
materials: 1 shallow box for the paper worth keeping
1 notebook and a pen, to write down who gave what
steps: Everyone sits down. One parcel opens at a time and the rest stay in their piles, and the rule holds for the adults too.
She opens hers. Torn paper goes in the trash bag as it comes off, and she smooths any sheet worth keeping flat into the shallow box.
Ribbon, wire ties and taped seams are yours. Cut them with the scissors before she pulls, then put the scissors back up.
She plays with it. Five minutes on the floor at least, before anyone touches the next parcel.
Write in the notebook with the pen: who gave what, and what she said when she saw it, in her words.
A sticky note on each new thing with the giver's name. Tape the box it came in back together so the thing has somewhere to live tonight.
main.tip: Stop when she stalls, even at three parcels in. The rest keep, and a pile saved for the 27th makes that whole morning.

outside.title: Who Else Is Out on Christmas Morning
paras: Get out before noon, when the street belongs to the few with a reason to be on it: somebody walking a dog in a coat, somebody riding a new bike with no gloves, a car packed to the roof and idling. Say hello to every one. Christmas morning is the one walk of the year where strangers answer.

days.infant: Kreston is 18 months, and the wrapping outranks what came in it for another year. Give him one parcel wrapped in two layers with nothing breakable inside and let the tearing take as long as it takes. Pretend play is starting, so a bow on his own head gets a laugh he goes back for five more times.

second.title: Everything Alive in This House
second.intro: She takes a clipboard round every room this afternoon and decides what counts as alive.
materials: 1 piece of stiff cardboard as a clipboard
steps: Tape a sheet of paper onto the cardboard. That is her clipboard and it stays in her hand for the hour.
Start in the kitchen and work through the house. One crayon mark per living thing. People count, and she will want a ruling on the fridge.
The new toy animals start an argument. Take her reasons and write them on her sheet in her words.

Back in one room, she splits them into groups she names. Two big squares of masking tape on the floor, and everything she can carry goes in the right one, houseplants included, apart from the ones that stay up on their shelves.
Anything too heavy to move gets a strip of tape beside it with her mark on it.
Now the photograph. Everything alive in one frame: plants carried in, a cat who declines, Kreston already leaving. Take six and keep the worst one.
Look at the picture and count who is missing. She will remember the plants upstairs.
second.tip: Say yes to her groups. Things with faces and things that stay still are working categories.

alternatives: Water every houseplant in the house, one cup each.
Line the new animals up biggest to smallest.
Draw the family, pets included, on one long sheet.
Count legs in the house, hers and everybody else's.
outAgain: The lakeshore, wrapped to the eyes, because the wind off the water is the point of going
A drive to the highest spot nearby, and stay in the warm car
The empty playground, cold slide and all
Grandparents, or whoever is closest with a kettle on
days.krestonPM: He will take the clipboard, so make him one from a spare piece of cardboard with a crayon taped to it. At 18 months he points and names, and the cat gets pointed at twenty times. Let him carry one houseplant to its square with both arms, and take the photograph on his terms.

insight.headline: Sorting living things is harder than sorting objects, because they move.
paras: Sorting blocks by color is a fixed problem. A cat that leaves, a brother who walks off, a plant that grows toward the window: those change while she is deciding about them. Children spend the years between three and six building the alive category, and they get there through motion first, then feeding, then growth. A toy dog with moving legs looks alive to her, and so does a stream. She sorts wrong for good reasons, and every ruling she makes out loud shows you how she is thinking. Ask her why the toy dog counts and you get the rule she is working from.

days.safety: Christmas packaging is the hazard today and Kreston is loose in it. Button batteries out of new toys go up and out of the house, wire ties and plastic film go straight into the trash bag, ribbon does not stay on the floor. The scissors stay with you. Check every new toy for parts that came loose in the box. Houseplant leaves and potting soil both go in his mouth at 18 months, so leave dieffenbachia, philodendron, pothos and peace lily up on their shelves and out of the sort, hand him a safe one to carry with both arms, and every pot goes back up the moment the photograph is done.

days.title: Ten Times Bigger
days.prepTonight: Flatten four to six of yesterday's boxes and stand them behind the sofa, and put the small toy she is likeliest to pick on the table on its own.

schedule.name: The Toy the Size of a Door

schedule.label: Get Outside

schedule.label: Second Main Event

opening.title: The Model on the Table
opening.need: one small toy from yesterday · paper · 1 marker.
steps: She picks one thing she got yesterday. Small, hers, and already carried round the house once.
Stand it alone in the middle of the table and list its parts out loud between you. Write every part she names down the page.
Ask how many boxes it would take to build one as tall as the door. Write her number at the bottom. You test it at 9:15.

main.title: The Toy the Size of a Door
materials: Heavy scissors or a craft knife (adult only)
The small original as the model
Her parts list from this morning
steps: Lay the flattened boxes across the floor and stand the original at the top, where she can see it from anywhere in the room.
Biggest part first. She points at it on the model, you cut the panel with the heavy scissors or the craft knife, and she stands back while you do.
Then part by part down her list. She looks at the original before each cut, and she is the one who says how big.
Packing tape holds the structure. Masking tape holds anything she may change her mind about, and she will change her mind twice.
Wrapping paper for the colored parts, torn and taped on in patches. Markers for the details she can see on the original and you cannot.
String for whatever hangs, ties or pulls. Stand it against the door and let her walk around it.
main.tip: Cut nothing she has not asked for. The wrong-looking proportions are her measurements.

outside.title: The Biggest Thing on the Street
paras: Go out hunting for the largest version of ordinary things: the tallest tree on the block, the biggest truck parked up, a flattened refrigerator box at the curb, the dog that comes up to her shoulder. Use her body as the ruler at three of them: waist, shoulder, over her head. December 26 puts more cardboard on the sidewalk than any other day of the year.

days.infant: Kreston is 18 months and climbing, and a door-sized cardboard shape is the most interesting thing in the house. Give him a wide offcut flat on the floor as his own island and he will stand on it, get off, and get back on. Pretend play means he feeds the big one a block. Keep him off the finished build until the tape has set.

second.title: The One That Fits in a Matchbox
second.intro: She makes it again, small enough to lose.
materials: Her parts list from this morning
steps: Empty the matchbox and push the tray out of the sleeve. Whatever she makes has to fit back inside with the lid closed.
Read her parts list back from this morning. Every part the enormous one has, the tiny one has.
Body first: a paper scrap folded or rolled to length, held with a strip of tape. You cut with the kitchen scissors, she folds.
The bottle cap does the work of one whole part. A head, a wheel, a base, whichever she names.
A thumbnail of foil for anything that shines.
Pencil for the marks too small for a crayon, crayons for the color.
Close the lid on it, then open it again, because she has to check it is still in there.
second.tip: Let her hold both at once, the door-sized one behind her and the matchbox in her fist. Same thing, same parts, two sizes apart.

alternatives: Draw the toy life-size on a flattened box and leave it flat.
Make a matchbox bed for it and nothing else.
Line up five things in the house biggest to smallest.
Trace round the big build on the floor with masking tape.
outAgain: A playground you have never been to, twenty minutes' drive, empty on the 26th
The woods, for the biggest tree the two of you can find
The nearest hill, for the view of how small the houses go
Indoor playground, or home with the biggest cardboard box the street produced
days.krestonPM: The matchbox and the bottle cap are choking hazards, so he works at the other end of the table with a shoebox, putting things in and taking them out. At 18 months that game outlasts anything you could buy him. At a new playground he wants the steps, holding one hand, up as many times as your back allows.

insight.headline: Making it enormous is how she checks she knows the parts.
paras: Azlyn can recognize her new toy from across a room and still not know how it is put together. Building it door-sized forces the question part by part, because a wrong-sized wing shows up at that scale and hides at three inches. Educators call this working at a different grain. She has to look at the original with real attention, and she has to hold the whole shape in her head while she works on one piece of it. The matchbox version this afternoon runs the same check from the other end, and it is fiddlier, so she slows down.

days.safety: The craft knife or the heavy scissors cutting big cardboard is adult-only work, and it happens with her standing back and knowing why. Christmas boxes carry staples in the seams, so run your hand along every panel before either child touches it. The scissors stay with you.

days.title: The Candle Rules
days.prepTonight: Set the metal tray on the table with the tea lights, the glass jar, the long spoon and a hair tie on it.

schedule.label: Get Outside

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: Carrying the Mugs to the Sink

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Wax Drips She Peels Off

schedule.name: Two Books and No Big Light

opening.title: The Tray, the Cloth and the Cup of Water
opening.need: 1 metal tray · 1 cup of water · 1 wet washcloth · 1 hair tie.
steps: Tie her hair back first, and say why while you do it.
She carries each thing to the table: tray in the middle, water and cloth on your side, inside your reach and not hers.
Ask what each is for. She gets the water first guess. Tell her the cloth smothers and leave that word with her until 9:15.

main.title: What a Flame Does
materials: 3 tea lights, or 1 dinner candle in a heavy holder
1 glass jar taller than the candle
steps: Tea lights on the tray, water and washcloth inside your reach, her hair in its tie. Both of you sit down, because nobody stands near a flame today.
Three rules: candles stay on the tray, only a grown-up strikes a match, tell a grown-up right away when something goes wrong. She says all three back.
Light one and put the matches back out of reach. She watches for a full minute with her hands under her legs.
Heat has a shape. Hold the metal spoon a hand's width above the flame for a count of ten, test the handle on your wrist, then let her feel it warm.
She blows it out. Watch the smoke rise in a line and fall apart. Relight it twice more.
Lower the glass jar over a lit one and watch it go out. Count the seconds. The wet washcloth does it faster.
main.tip: Say yes every time she asks to light it again. A flame she may look at loses its pull.

outside.title: Her Shadow, Longer Than She Is
paras: The sun stays low all day this week, so her shadow runs long at eleven in the morning. Find pale sidewalk in full sun, stand her at one end, and pace out her shadow in your feet, then hers. Turn her to face the sun and watch it swap ends.

days.infant: Kreston is 18 months, and a flame at his eye level is the one thing today he has no safe part in. Run the hour with him behind a closed door with another adult, or in the high chair the far end of the table with the tray pulled to your side. Outside he chases his own shadow and cannot work out why it stays attached.

second.title: The Handle Turns In
second.intro: The stove gets the candle's treatment: a line on the floor, rules out loud, and a real job at the end of them.
materials: Masking tape for the floor line
A cup of cooled milk for Kreston
steps: Masking tape across the floor an arm's length back from the stove. Past it belongs to whoever is cooking.
Milk, cocoa and sugar into the cold pan, off the heat. She measures, she pours, she gets cocoa on the counter.
Pan onto a front burner with the back burners empty and off, handle turned in and never out over the room. Have her check it.
Step stool to the stove, the one crossing of the tape line all day. Your hand on the pan handle, your arm behind her back, and she stirs with the wooden spoon.
Off the heat the moment it steams. Boiled cocoa skins over and she will not drink it.
Pour the two mugs. Stir a spoonful into Kreston's cup of cooled milk so he has what everyone else has.
Everyone drinks it on the far side of the tape line.
second.tip: Give her the whole stirring job and stay quiet. The cocoa is the excuse.

alternatives: Cold cocoa shaken in a lidded jar.
Melt a square of chocolate in a warm spoon.
Draw the three candle rules for the fridge.
Tape the floor line and practice standing behind it.
outAgain: The green space with a ball, because everyone here needs to run after three days indoors
The riverside path, hats on, twenty minutes each way
A walk to see whose tree is still up and whose is at the curb
The yard or the garage, kicking a ball at a wall
days.krestonPM: Give him his cup of cooled milk in the high chair before the pan comes off the heat, so he is boxed in for the hot part. At 18 months he kicks a ball with a real swing of the leg, so put one in front of him and stand back.

insight.headline: Fire and flame need rules, not avoidance.
paras: A child who has never been near a flame with you is the one who tries it alone in a bedroom. That is the argument for doing it together, with the matches back out of reach afterward. Fire takes skin in under a second and a house from one curtain, so the handling happens on a metal tray, water and a wet cloth inside your reach. She learned three rules this morning by saying them out loud, and she has watched a jar starve a flame of air. Give her the real jobs: blowing out, smothering, carrying the unlit candle. Say yes to the birthday candles, the menorah and the stove, hands close and rules short.

days.safety: Open flame, matches and hot wax at 9:15, hot milk on a stove at 1:00, and an 18-month-old who pulls himself up on counters. The matches go back out of reach between every strike, on a high shelf and never the table. The heated spoon stays bowl end in your hand, because that end holds the heat long after the handle is warm. She touches the handle and nothing else, and the spoon goes on the tray to cool. Never leave the tea lights burning in an empty room. Kreston is behind a door or in the high chair for both.

days.title: The Print It Leaves Behind
days.prepTonight: Stand the block of clay and a folded stack of newspaper on the table. Buy a small cake and a tub of frosting while you are out, for Wednesday.

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Ten Prints in a Row

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Bath and the Print of Her Own Hand

opening.title: What Has a Pattern Underneath
opening.need: 1 fork · 1 shallow bowl · ten minutes of the house · her.
steps: Turn a fork over and show her the back of it, then the sole of her shoe. Both carry a pattern.
Send her round the house for ten things with a pattern underneath: a comb, a coin, a bottle cap, a key, a big leaf.
Line them up in the bowl in the order she found them. Every one leaves a copy of itself behind by lunchtime.

main.title: The Clay Keeps the Shape
materials: 1 block modeling clay or air-dry clay
A stack of newspaper, folded into a pad
1 wooden spoon, for the fine work
steps: Fold the newspaper into a pad the size of a placemat. Everything happens on top of that, because clay picks up whatever it is lying on.
Warm the clay between your palms until it gives, then roll ten pucks the width of her hand and press each flat, about a finger thick. One puck per object.
First object face down onto the first puck, and she presses it home with the flat of both thumbs, middle first and then out to the edges.
Back of the wooden spoon round the rim, rubbed slow. The comb teeth and the letters round the coin come up sharp.
Lift the object straight up while she holds the puck down with her other hand. A sideways pull drags the print out of shape.
Marker on the back of each: her initial, and a number matching its place in the line. All ten face up along the counter until 1:00.
main.tip: Press one object twice, once light and once hard, and lay the pair side by side. The hard one is the print she can still read after it has been buried.

outside.title: Prints in the Frost
paras: Morning frost sits on grass, car roofs and every shaded patch the low sun misses. Walk her across a white lawn and turn round to look at her boot trail. Find a set that is not hers: a dog, a bird, a bike tire. Press her hand on a frosted hood and count how long the print lasts. Everything out here loses its print by lunchtime, and the ten on the counter are not going anywhere.

days.infant: Kreston is 18 months and a pinch of clay goes straight in his mouth, so his part is one puck too big to swallow, held down under your hands and taken back into your pocket after. Press his whole hand into it, lift it out together, and write his name on the back while he watches. In the frost he stamps, looks, and stamps again in the same spot.

second.title: Digging Up What She Made
second.intro: The ten prints are done, and now they go under the oats.
materials: Index cards or card cut to size
1 sheet of thick paper, for the December handprint
Washable non-toxic poster paint and 1 wide soft brush
1 wet washcloth in a shallow bowl
steps: Oats into the deep tray three fingers deep, on the kitchen floor and off the carpet.
She turns her back. Bury the ten prints at different depths and rake the surface flat.
Show her once and hand it over: the spoon moves the oats, the brush clears the last of it. Dig wide, brush close.
Every print comes out face down. She turns it over, says what made it, then checks against the object.
Line the prints along the floor with their objects beside them.

One index card per print. She dictates and you write it with the marker, word for word: the bottom of my shoe. Then swap, and she buries them for you and stands over the tray telling you where you are wrong.

The December handprint last, on paper, while the oats go back in their bag. Paint her palm with the brush rather than dipping her hand. Press flat, count to three, lift straight up, then Kreston's beside hers with the washcloth already in your hand. Write December, her 4 and his 18 months next to the pair.
second.tip: Sift the oats back into their bag. They get buried and dug out a dozen more times before they go gray.

alternatives: Bury the prints in dry rice and use fingers.
Rub a crayon over paper laid on each object instead, for a second set.
Match the ten objects to the ten prints, face up.
Stand two of the prints on the windowsill where the low sun rakes across them.
outAgain: Swimming, the last one of the year and the fifty-second
Indoor playground, if the pool is shut for the holidays
The library, for the books that have to go back before January
A warm café and a window, if nobody has the energy for a swimsuit
days.krestonPM: He swims too, at 18 months walking into the shallow end with both your hands and no idea water is different. Twenty minutes and out before he is cold. Hold him chest to chest for the first minute so the pool noise arrives with your face in front of him.

insight.headline: A copy of a thing teaches her what a fossil is.
paras: Azlyn has looked at dinosaur bones all year without any idea how they got to be inside a rock. This morning she made ten of them: something soft took a shape, the object went away, and the shape stayed. That sequence is the whole idea, and she owns it because her hands did each step in order. The frost outside made the same prints and lost them by lunchtime, and that is the other half of it. Museums hand her the finished fossil. Pressing a shoe sole into clay hands her the process, and by Friday she will use the word on a rock in the yard.

days.safety: Clay is not food and an 18-month-old will test that, so Kreston's piece is one puck too big to swallow, it stays under your hands, and it comes back to your pocket before he is put down. Pinch every loose crumb off the floor at the end. A tray of dry oats at floor height is a choking risk, so it goes on the counter the moment you step away. The coin and the bottle cap in her ten are choke-sized, so they get counted out onto the pad and counted back into the bowl, and he is in the high chair for the dig. Washable non-toxic paint only. Everybody washes hands before food. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

days.title: Mom's Day Off
days.prepTonight: Stand the cake, the frosting, the sprinkles and the candles on the counter, and put one wrappable thing from the house in a bag by the door.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: One of Every Kind in a Row

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Lights Left On in the Daytime

opening.title: Everything Sweet in the House
opening.need: 1 large tray or baking sheet · her · three trips.
steps: Sit down on the sofa. That is your first job of the day and it holds until the walk.
Send her for every piece of candy in the house. Stockings, the cupboard, the bowl by the door, coat pockets. The top of the fridge is yours, pointed out from the sofa.
It all lands on the tray at your feet. She makes three trips and finds things you forgot you hid.

main.title: One of Every Kind in a Row
materials: Every piece of candy in the house
Paper and a marker for labels
steps: Tip the tray out on the floor in front of her. You stay on the sofa the whole hour.
One kind per cup of the muffin tin. Her categories, so everything gold may end up together.
Count each cup out loud with her. She says the number, you write it on the paper with the marker.
She names each group. Write her name for it, tear the paper into labels, tape one to each cup.
Lay one of every kind in a row along the empty tray.
One sandwich bag per person, labeled and taped shut. She deals the shares out and decides what fair means. Kreston's goes on a high shelf, unopened.
main.tip: Do not fix her groups. Gold-wrapped things belong together if she says so.

outside.title: The Lights Left On in the Daytime
paras: Half the street has left its lights on in daylight this week and they look washed out at eleven in the morning. Walk the block counting lit windows, then count the same houses again from the front window at 5:45, with the light gone and dinner on the way. It is your birthday, so Azlyn pushes Kreston for a whole block.

days.infant: Kreston is 18 months and cannot have a single thing on that floor, so give him two of the small bowls and a wooden spoon in the high chair, up out of the candy and in your sightline. Filling and emptying is his game of the month. He will want a bag too, so tape one shut with a board book inside.

second.title: The Birthday Azlyn Runs
second.intro: Azlyn runs this from the frosting to the singing, and the one adult job is lighting the candles.
materials: 1 store-bought cake or plain loaf cake
1 knife for cutting the cake (adult only)
One thing from the house to wrap
steps: Cake onto the plate. She spreads the frosting with her fingers and nobody smooths it after her.
Sprinkles next, the whole shaker, from whatever height she chooses. What lands on the plate stays on the plate.
Paper and crayons on the floor for the card. Nobody tells her what to draw.
The present: the thing from the house, wrapped in newspaper, taped by her, ribbon tied by you because a bow beats her fingers.
Candles in. She spaces them and counts them. You strike the matches, the only part she does not do.
She calls everyone to the table and says where each person sits, including you, on your own birthday.
Singing, blowing out, and the first slice is yours. She reads the card out loud and it will not match the drawing.
second.tip: Let it be worse than you would have made it. A lopsided cake and a present off your own shelf is the gift.

alternatives: Store cake, candles in, straight to the singing.
She makes the card and nothing else.
A tea party with the good cups and no cake at all.
Everyone draws Mom, and she picks the best one.
outAgain: The indoor play center, and you sit down with a coffee while somebody else's noise happens
The library, warm and quiet, and she picks your book
A café with cake, on the grounds that there is no such thing as too much
Home on the sofa, if the birthday you want is a quiet one
days.krestonPM: At 18 months he is in the birthday for real. He claps when the singing starts and blows before anybody else. Pretend play is coming in, so he feeds the cake to a toy. Keep the lit candles at the far side of the table from his chair.

insight.headline: Sorting the candy is more interesting to her than eating it.
paras: Hand a four-year-old a pile of mixed candy and watch what happens first. She lines it up. Children this age run a private census of the world, grouping and regrouping, and a heap of wrappers with colors, sizes and shapes in it is richer material than most toys sold for the purpose. The counting, the naming of groups and the one-of-each row are all real math, and she will do twenty minutes of it without you asking once, then come back to the tin after lunch. The eating comes after, and it comes slower, because she has an interest in the collection staying whole. The wrappers go into a bag she guards for a week after the candy is gone.

days.safety: Hard candy, chocolate coins and foil wrappers across the floor are a choking hazard for an 18-month-old, so he spends the sorting hour in the high chair with his bowls, and the floor gets swept before he is down. Lit candles on a cake sit at his eye level and he will reach. Put his chair on the far side and blow them out early. The cake knife is yours, and it goes back in the drawer as soon as the slices are cut.

days.title: The Table of Everybody
days.prepTonight: Find six to ten printed photos tonight, one of everybody including anyone who has died, and cut thick card into strips. No prints means she draws them tomorrow.

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: Letters to the People in the Photos

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Photo Box on Her Lap

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Last Books of the Year

opening.title: Naming Everybody Out Loud
steps: Ask her to name everybody in the family. Write every name in the order she says it, and add nobody she has not named.
Read the list back. She remembers three more, one a friend from swimming and one somebody's dog.
Ask who is missing. The people who have died come up here, or at 9:15, and either is fine.

main.title: The Photographs Standing Up
materials: 6–10 printed photos (or drawings of the people, if there are no prints)
Thick card cut into folding stands
1 battery tea light, or a flashlight under a jar
steps: She picks the spot. A side table, a tray on a shelf, the end of the bookcase, out of the traffic and off the floor.
Cloth over it. She straightens it until she is satisfied.
One photo per name on her list. Anyone with no print, she draws on card.
Fold each card strip into an L, tape a photo to the upright, stand it up. She says each name out loud.
Marker under each stand: the name. She writes the letters she knows and you fill in the rest.

Battery tea light in the middle, or the flashlight face up under a jar. No flame on this table, and she switches it on herself. The greenery from the 10:30 walk goes round the base at 11:15, once you are both home with it.
main.tip: The people who have died get a stand the same size as everyone else's. She will ask a direct question. Answer it in one plain sentence, keep working, and expect it again four times this week.

outside.title: Cutting Green for the Table
paras: Take a bag and the kitchen scissors, which stay in your hand, and bring back a handful of green for the table. She picks each sprig and you cut it. Pine and spruce are the easy ones at the end of December, and both smell of themselves when she crushes a needle. A cedar sprig off a low branch holds its shape for a week. Cut low, cut little, and ask before taking from a neighbor's yard.

days.infant: Kreston is 18 months and will have a photo stand off that table within the hour, so tape a spare photo of himself onto a card strip. He carries it around and turns it to face people, a new skill this month. On the walk he holds a sprig of pine and arrives with it in pieces.

second.title: Letters to the People in the Photos
second.intro: The table is full of people who are somewhere else, and the mail still runs tomorrow.
materials: 1 pen for you to take dictation
steps: Go round the table and pick out the living ones. Those are the letters. She will want to write to the others too, so say the truth: those stay on the table.
One folded card per person, drawn in crayon first. She decides who gets which drawing.
She dictates and you write it in pen, word for word, including the part that makes no sense.
She picks a sticker to seal each envelope, one per person.
Address them from your list. She puts the stamp on, top right corner, pressed with her thumb.
The stack goes in her hands to the post office at 2:30, and she mails them one at a time.
Anything she has not finished stays on the table for 4:00 and goes out tomorrow.
second.tip: Photograph each card before it goes in the envelope. Two of those people will keep hers on the fridge for a year.

alternatives: One card to one person, and stop there.
Call two of them on video and let her hold the phone.
Draw the whole family on one long sheet.
Sort the photo box by who is in each picture.
outAgain: The post office, with the letters in her hands and the slot at her height
The mailbox on the corner, if the counter line is out the door
The grocery store for tomorrow, and she carries one thing
A walk past the houses with the photos still in the windows
days.krestonPM: At 18 months a post office is a room full of lines and strangers, so twenty minutes is the budget. Give him one envelope to hold and he carries it like a job. He climbs the step there holding the rail, one foot at a time, new this month.

insight.headline: A photo on a table gives a dead person a place, and that helps her more than an explanation.
paras: At four, Azlyn still hears death as a temporary state and asks when the person is coming back. Abstract answers slide off her, and she will ask again in a week whatever you say. A photo on a covered table gives her something she can handle: a spot in the house where that person is, a name she says out loud, greenery she chose herself laid round the base. Grief researchers who work with young children lean on rituals for this reason. She gets to include somebody, the part she was asking for underneath the question. Set the table up once and leave it standing as long as she wants it.

days.safety: Yew is poisonous in every part, and holly and mistletoe berries make a small child sick, and Kreston mouths everything he picks up, so cut pine, spruce or cedar only and go through the bag before it comes indoors. No berries on that table at all. The battery tea light needs its screws done up tight, because a button battery swallowed at 18 months is a surgical emergency.
